hints: Focus on carbon counting first, since butanoic acid has a four carbon chain with the $\text{-COOH}$ group.
Check how many carbons each starting material would give in the acid product, remembering nitriles and alcohols gain or keep carbons in predictable ways.
Look for the starting material that already contains the four carbon butanoate skeleton, just needing a proton to become the acid.
walkthrough:
**Identify the target**

Butanoic acid is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$. It is a straight chain carboxylic acid with 4 carbons in total.

Target:
$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$$

**Recall the three key routes to acids**

A carboxylate salt plus strong acid gives the acid back. A nitrile hydrolysed gives an acid with the same number of carbons as the nitrile. A primary alcohol oxidised gives an acid with the same number of carbons.

Rules:
$$\text{RCOO}^- + \text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{RCOOH}$$
$$\text{RCN} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{RCOOH} + \text{NH}_3$$

**Count carbons in each option**

Option A already has $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COO}^-$, which is 4 carbons. Options B, C and D all lead to the wrong chain length, as we will see.

Check:
$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CN} = 5 \text{ carbons} \rightarrow \text{pentanoic acid}$$
$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH} = 3 \text{ carbons} \rightarrow \text{propanoic acid}$$

**Conclude the working method**

Adding a strong acid to sodium butanoate protonates it directly to butanoic acid. This is a simple acid-base reaction with no change in carbon skeleton.

Equation:
$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{Na} + \text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H} + \text{NaCl}$$

options.A: Sodium butanoate contains the butanoate ion, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COO}^-$. Reaction with a strong acid such as dilute HCl protonates it to give $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$, which is butanoic acid. Carbon skeleton is unchanged.
options.B: Acid hydrolysis of a nitrile gives a carboxylic acid with the same total carbon count, including the CN carbon. $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CN}$ has 5 carbons, so it gives pentanoic acid, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$, not butanoic acid.
options.C: Acidic hydrolysis of the ester $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ splits it into the acid part and alcohol part. The acid part is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$, propanoic acid (3 carbons), plus propan-1-ol. Students who count the total carbons in the ester (6) often pick this by mistake.
options.D: Strong oxidation of a primary alcohol gives the carboxylic acid with the same number of carbons. $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ is propan-1-ol (3 carbons), so it oxidises to propanoic acid, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$, which is one carbon short of butanoic acid.
